findings.text: The first paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. A newcomer can say what it is and why it matters without reading further.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: prerequisites, clone, install and a first command, plus a description of what happens when you run it. The top of the page links straight to them ("Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself").
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" / "./setup.sh" / "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page title and nearly all of its body are about firstmate, not Athena. The heading "Start here" starts firstmate material, so a newcomer who came for Athena may think they are on the wrong page or skim past the Athena information.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; heading "Start here"

findings.text: The page never shows this main feature: no example request, commit, cost record or check verdict. The firstmate study only shows that Athena can read and explain a codebase, which is a side ability, so the main promise is stated but not shown.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: A newcomer will not know whose decisions these are or why they would be asked to make one. The link seems meant for the project owner and is confusing near the top of a first-visit page.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The middle of the page is dense, specialist material: twelve transition cards, guards, exit codes and 45 claims. It is careful and every statement is traced to a source, but it is far more than a newcomer needs to judge Athena. Nothing says how much of it is worth reading.
"About this page" refers to a repository folder the newcomer has not seen. It explains nothing useful to a first-time reader.
findings.source: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: The page openly says the study only read the code and never ran it. This builds trust, but it is placed after the glossary, near the end of the page, where a newcomer is unlikely to reach it.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
